practice.stem: Selective toxicity means that an antimicrobial:
options: Is chosen only after culture and sensitivity results return
Acts more strongly against the microorganism than against the patient
Works against only one species of bacteria, so normal flora are always spared
Has no effect on human cells or on the patient's normal flora
practice.rationale: Selective toxicity exploits differences between bacterial and human cells so the drug hits the bug harder than the patient. Her key concept: "selective does not mean harmless" — allergy, tissue damage and flora disruption still happen. Working on one species describes a narrow spectrum, not selectivity.

practice.stem: Which statement about broad-spectrum antibiotics is correct?
options: They cover a wider range of organisms but expose more normal flora and add selection pressure
They are less likely than narrow-spectrum drugs to promote resistance
They are more powerful than narrow-spectrum drugs against any single organism
They are always the best choice once the organism is known, because they leave nothing uncovered
practice.rationale: "Broad spectrum doesn't mean more powerful, it just means it can kill more different kinds." Broad coverage kills more normal flora (diarrhea, yeast, C. diff) and is the most likely to promote resistance; once the bug is known, narrow is preferred.

practice.stem: A bacterium survives an antibiotic by pumping the drug back out of the cell. This resistance mechanism is:
options: Reduced entry
Drug inactivation
Target alteration
Efflux
practice.rationale: Efflux = the bacterium pumps the drug out. Inactivation is an enzyme destroying the drug (β-lactamase); target alteration means the drug binds poorly (MRSA's PBPs); reduced entry keeps the drug from getting in at all.

practice.stem: Which statement about antibiotic resistance matches the lecture?
options: The bacteria become resistant; the patient does not become "resistant to antibiotics"
Only broad-spectrum antibiotics can promote resistance
Patients who take many antibiotics become resistant to them, so their doses must be increased
Antibiotic exposure teaches each bacterium how to resist
practice.rationale: "It's the bacteria themselves that are resistant. It's not the patient." Resistant mutants may already be present and the drug favors them (selection pressure) — it doesn't teach them. All antimicrobials can promote resistance; broad ones are just more likely to.

practice.stem: About how long does a culture take to identify the organism?
options: 2 weeks
24–48 hours
15–20 minutes
5–7 days
practice.rationale: Culture takes 24–48 hours, so patients are often started on broad therapy first. The Gram stain (gram-positive vs gram-negative) comes back in about 15–20 minutes.

practice.stem: According to the lecture, how common is true penicillin allergy?
options: About 10% report it, but only about 1% are truly allergic
About 1% report it and nearly all of them are truly allergic
About 50% report it, but only about 10% are truly allergic
About 30% report it and about 10% are truly allergic
practice.rationale: 10% report a penicillin allergy; ~1% are truly allergic — often what's reported is a side effect like diarrhea. (30% is the share of people who carry S. aureus.)

practice.stem: Which drug is paired with piperacillin to protect it from β-lactamases?
options: Clavulanate
Sulfamethoxazole
Cilastatin
Tazobactam
practice.rationale: Piperacillin + tazobactam = Zosyn. Clavulanate is paired with amoxicillin (Augmentin). Cilastatin protects imipenem from a kidney enzyme, not a bacterial one; sulfamethoxazole is the partner of trimethoprim.

practice.stem: Why does vancomycin work against MRSA when most β-lactams don't?
options: It binds MRSA's altered PBPs more tightly than penicillin or amoxicillin can
It blocks β-lactamase so the penicillin can work
It inhibits the bacterial 50S ribosome
It binds peptidoglycan building blocks instead of penicillin-binding proteins
practice.rationale: Vancomycin is a glycopeptide, not a β-lactam — it "works elsewhere in cell construction," so MRSA's altered PBPs don't matter. Binding the altered PBP describes ceftaroline; blocking β-lactamase is clavulanate/tazobactam.

practice.stem: What is the role of cilastatin in imipenem/cilastatin (Primaxin)?
options: It is a second antibiotic added to cover MRSA, which imipenem misses
It blocks the kidney enzyme that would inactivate imipenem
It prevents seizures caused by imipenem
It inhibits bacterial β-lactamases
practice.rationale: Cilastatin inhibits a renal enzyme the body normally uses to break down imipenem — "fighting against the body's metabolism," not the bacteria. It isn't a β-lactamase inhibitor, carbapenems don't cover MRSA, and it doesn't prevent seizures.

practice.stem: Bacteriostatic antibiotics depend on what to clear an infection?
options: High peak drug levels
A second bactericidal antibiotic
An acidic stomach
A functioning immune system
practice.rationale: Bacteriostatic drugs only suppress growth — "functioning immune system required!" — so the immune system can "catch up" and finish the job. That's why she avoids them in immunocompromised patients.

practice.stem: Linezolid is usually reserved for which organisms?
options: MRSA and vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE)
Influenza A and B within 48 hours of symptoms
Pseudomonas and anaerobes in mixed abdominal infections
Intestinal C. difficile after clindamycin
practice.rationale: "Let's protect this antibiotic" — linezolid is kept for MRSA and VRE, so "if your patient is on this, they probably have one of these, or maybe both." Pseudomonas is the Zosyn/cefepime/cipro connection.

practice.stem: How long must a patient avoid alcohol with metronidazole?
options: Only on the days a dose is taken
During treatment and for at least 3 days after the last dose
For 24 hours after the last dose
Alcohol is fine as long as each dose is taken with a full meal
practice.rationale: Alcohol causes an Antabuse-like reaction ("if you drink it, you get sick"), and enough drug remains for at least three days after the final dose. Propylene glycol products are avoided too.

practice.stem: Which set of adverse effects is characteristic of amphotericin B?
options: Nephrotoxicity, hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia
Tendon rupture, dysglycemia and QT prolongation
Tooth discoloration and photosensitivity
Serotonin syndrome and thrombocytopenia
practice.rationale: Ampho B damages the kidneys and wastes K⁺ and Mg²⁺ (plus anemia, liver enzymes and infusion reactions) — the Nephron meme. Tendons/glucose/QT is cipro; teeth and sun is doxycycline; serotonin syndrome and platelets is linezolid.

practice.stem: How does oseltamivir (Tamiflu) work?
options: Blocks synthesis of the cell wall that influenza viruses need
Kills influenza viruses directly by breaking their outer membrane
Inhibits neuraminidase, so new viruses aren't released to spread
Works like a vaccine, building antibodies against influenza
practice.rationale: Oseltamivir inhibits viral neuraminidase, limiting release and spread. Antivirals suppress replication rather than kill the virus, and oseltamivir is not a vaccine.

practice.stem: The nurse is about to hang the first dose of an IV antibiotic. A urine culture is ordered but hasn't been collected. What should the nurse do?
options: Cancel the culture because the antibiotic is broad spectrum
Hold the antibiotic until the culture result returns
Collect the urine culture first, then give the dose without delay
Give the antibiotic now and collect the culture with the next void
practice.rationale: "Once the first dose of antibiotics goes into the patient, then our results are not accurate." Cultures come before the first dose as long as that doesn't delay treatment — so collect it now, not after, and don't wait 24–48 h for the result.

practice.stem: A patient started on broad piperacillin/tazobactam has a culture back at 48 hours: the organism is susceptible to a narrower drug and the patient is improving. What should the nurse anticipate?
options: Continuing Zosyn because the patient is improving
Narrowing to targeted therapy based on culture and susceptibility
Adding a second broad-spectrum antibiotic
Stopping all antibiotics now, since the organism has been identified
practice.rationale: Empiric therapy is "the best guess"; when results return the regimen is reassessed — continue, narrow, change or stop. Narrowing to the targeted drug spares normal flora and selection pressure.

practice.stem: A patient says, "I'm allergic to penicillin — it gave me diarrhea." What is the best interpretation?
options: The patient will be allergic to every antibiotic
This is a true allergy, so all penicillins and cephalosporins are now contraindicated for life
Diarrhea is a common side effect, not an allergy; the nurse should clarify and document the details
This is anaphylaxis and requires desensitization
practice.rationale: "Oh, I got diarrhea. No, well, that's actually a side effect and not an allergy." Only about 1% of those who report penicillin allergy are truly allergic; ask what happened, when, and how severe it was.

practice.stem: Ten days into broad-spectrum antibiotics, a patient develops white patches in the mouth. The nurse recognizes:
options: A sign that the antibiotic is working against the infection
Antibiotic resistance that has developed in the patient
An allergic reaction that requires stopping all antibiotics now
A superinfection — normal flora killed, letting yeast flourish
practice.rationale: Superinfection is a new infection during treatment of the first; killing normal flora lets a second agent (yeast, C. diff) take over, especially with broad drugs and long courses. Patients don't become resistant — bacteria do.

practice.stem: A patient with a documented history of throat swelling after amoxicillin has a new order for a cephalosporin. What should the nurse do?
options: Give it with an antacid to prevent a reaction
Give it — cephalosporins are a different class, so there's no cross-reaction risk at all
Substitute amoxicillin/clavulanate instead
Recognize possible cross-sensitivity and clarify with the provider before giving it
practice.rationale: A true penicillin allergy means all penicillins (Augmentin included) and "some cross-sensitivity" with cephalosporins. She said look first for something with no risk; it may still be used for a severe infection, but that's the provider's call after you raise it.

practice.stem: Oral vancomycin is ordered for a patient with MRSA bacteremia. What is the nurse's concern?
options: Oral vancomycin is not absorbed, so it won't treat a bloodstream infection
Oral vancomycin is too nephrotoxic to use in a bloodstream infection like this
Oral vancomycin should be given with calcium
Vancomycin doesn't work against MRSA
practice.rationale: "Route is really important": oral vanco stays in the intestine and treats intestinal C. diff; systemic MRSA needs IV vanco. Vancomycin does cover MRSA.

practice.stem: A patient's IV vancomycin is due at 1800, and a trough level is ordered. When should the trough be drawn?
options: At any time during the infusion
Just before the 1800 dose
30 minutes after the 1800 infusion ends
Two hours after the 1800 dose
practice.rationale: The trough is the lowest point — drawn right before the next dose. A peak is usually ~30 minutes after an IV infusion. High troughs predict kidney damage better than high peaks.

practice.stem: A patient starting doxycycline says, "I'll take it at bedtime with a sip of water so I don't forget." The best response is:
options: "Bedtime is best — lying down lets it absorb more slowly and gently."
"Take it with a full glass of water and stay upright for 30 minutes — not right before bed."
"That's fine, as long as you take it with a full glass of milk to protect your stomach lining."
"Crush it into applesauce at bedtime so it's easier to swallow."
practice.rationale: Doxycycline irritates and can ulcerate the esophagus: full glass of water, upright ≥ 30 minutes, not immediately before bed. Milk and calcium bind it and reduce absorption.

practice.stem: A patient on doxycycline takes a daily calcium supplement and an antacid. What should the nurse teach?
options: Take them together, and double the doxycycline dose to make up for the binding
Separate them from doxycycline by a few hours; they don't need to be stopped
Stop the calcium and antacid permanently
Take them all together to protect the stomach
practice.rationale: Aluminum, calcium, iron and magnesium bind doxycycline in the gut. Her answer to the student: you don't have to stop them — "usually they say 2–3 hours" apart.

practice.stem: Which patient prescribed azithromycin is at highest risk for a dysrhythmia?
options: A man with a normal ECG who takes the drug with food and no other medications
A woman who takes the drug with food
A man with a penicillin allergy
A woman with a low potassium who also takes another QT-prolonging drug
practice.rationale: QT risk rises with other QT drugs, low K⁺ or Mg²⁺ and existing rhythm problems — and "women are automatically at increased risk because at baseline we have a longer QT interval." Food and penicillin allergy don't matter here.

practice.stem: On day 6 of clindamycin, a patient has six watery stools, abdominal cramping and a temperature of 38.4°C. What should the nurse do?
options: Give an over-the-counter antidiarrheal and recheck tomorrow
Encourage the patient to finish the clindamycin course first, then report it
Document it as an expected, harmless side effect
Report the findings promptly and not give an antidiarrheal on her own
practice.rationale: "Clinda → C. diff." Watery or bloody stools, cramping or fever during or after clindamycin need to be reported, and significant diarrhea isn't treated independently with antidiarrheals.

practice.stem: A patient started on linezolid also takes sertraline (an SSRI). Which findings should the nurse watch for?
options: Tinnitus, vertigo, hearing loss and balance problems
Tooth discoloration, photosensitivity, heartburn and nausea
Metallic taste, darkened urine and a headache
Agitation, confusion, diaphoresis, tremor, fever, rigidity
practice.rationale: Linezolid has MAO-inhibitor activity, so with SSRIs/SNRIs it can cause serotonin syndrome — those are the signs on slide 49. Tinnitus and vertigo are gentamicin; metallic taste is metronidazole; teeth and sun are doxycycline.

practice.stem: A 74-year-old taking prednisone is on ciprofloxacin and reports new pain and swelling at the back of the ankle. The nurse should:
options: Recommend an antacid with each dose
Tell her to walk it off and keep taking the drug
Report it promptly — it may be tendinitis or impending tendon rupture
Recognize it as an expected effect of the prednisone alone and continue both
practice.rationale: Fluoroquinolones cause tendinitis and rupture, usually the Achilles, and older age plus corticosteroids raise the risk. Tendon pain or swelling is reported promptly.

practice.stem: Which instruction is correct for nystatin oral suspension for thrush?
options: Use it to treat systemic fungal infections
Take it with an antacid to protect it from stomach acid
Swallow it quickly so it reaches the bloodstream
Swish it around the mouth and hold it before swallowing
practice.rationale: Nystatin is inactivated once it hits stomach acid, so it's "really a topical medication" — it has to stay in contact with the mouth. It is not for systemic infection.

practice.stem: A patient on a protein-synthesis inhibitor is severely immunocompromised. Why might the provider prefer a bactericidal drug?
options: Bacteriostatic drugs cause osmotic lysis
Bacteriostatic drugs rely on the immune system to finish clearing the bacteria
Bactericidal drugs never cause adverse effects
Bactericidal drugs are always narrower in spectrum, so they spare the normal flora
practice.rationale: "You really don't want to use bacteriostatic drugs with patients who are immunocompromised, because you're banking on the immune system to do the last bit." Static vs cidal isn't a ranking of strength; osmotic lysis is the cell-wall drugs.

practice.stem: A patient starting TMP-SMX has no heart or liver failure. Which fluid instruction is correct?
options: Avoid drinking water within 2 hours of each dose
Drink plenty of fluids to help prevent kidney crystals
Limit fluids so the drug stays concentrated in the urine
Fluid intake doesn't matter with this antibiotic
practice.rationale: TMP-SMX can cause kidney injury and crystalluria, especially when dehydrated — "unless they have a contraindication… heart failure or liver failure… go for it."

practice.stem: Order: imipenem/cilastatin IV. Home medications: valproic acid. What is the safety concern?
options: Imipenem can lower valproic acid levels → breakthrough seizures; alert the provider
The combination causes hyperkalemia; check potassium before each dose
No significant interaction; give both medications as scheduled
Valproic acid raises imipenem to toxic levels → kidney injury; hold the valproic acid
practice.rationale: Carbapenems substantially reduce valproic acid concentrations, and a falling level is "one of the biggest risks for having a huge, horrible seizure." Identify valproic acid use before the first dose.

practice.stem: Order: ceftriaxone IV now. The patient has one peripheral IV, with a calcium-containing IV solution running. What should the nurse do?
options: Not Y-site them: stop the solution, flush the line, give the ceftriaxone, or use a separate line
Piggyback it into the calcium solution, but run the ceftriaxone faster so it can't react
Piggyback the ceftriaxone into the running solution
Mix the ceftriaxone directly into the solution bag
practice.rationale: Ceftriaxone + calcium forms a precipitate that can deposit in the lungs and kidneys. Never run two things in one line without checking compatibility — separate lumens, or give, stop, flush, then give.

practice.stem: Day 4 of IV vancomycin plus gentamicin. Creatinine 0.9 → 1.3 → 1.8 mg/dL; urine output 20 mL/h for 3 hours. What is the nurse's priority?
options: Report the rising creatinine and falling urine output before the next doses
Give both doses on time; kidney values usually settle once the infection clears
Encourage extra calcium in the diet to protect the kidneys
Draw a peak level 2 hours after the vancomycin dose instead
practice.rationale: Both drugs are nephrotoxic and together raise the risk. "A trend of anything is better than a one-time reading" — a rising creatinine and falling urine output are the kidney findings to report.

practice.stem: Order: TMP-SMX DS PO. Medications: lisinopril (an ACE inhibitor, which raises potassium). Today's K⁺: 5.6 mEq/L (high). The nurse should:
options: Hold and notify the provider — two K⁺-raising drugs and a high K⁺
Give the dose with a potassium supplement as usual
Give the dose; ACE inhibitors lower potassium, so it balances out
Give it with an antacid to reduce how much is absorbed
practice.rationale: "Put together this [raises] potassium with the patients on other medications that raise potassium. Now our risk is increasing." A high K⁺ before the dose is the finding to report.

practice.stem: Order: oseltamivir PO. A healthy 30-year-old outpatient reports flu symptoms began 72 hours ago. What should the nurse do?
options: Give it and tell her it will cure the flu in a day or two
Tell the provider symptoms began 72 h ago — benefit is greatest within 48 h
Give the live intranasal flu vaccine today instead, since it's past 48 hours
Give it together with an antibiotic for her cold symptoms
practice.rationale: "Within 48 hours is really the cutoff"; after that "you're really not going to get enough benefit." Severe, hospitalized or high-risk patients may still benefit later — she has none of those. It doesn't cure, and it may interfere with the live intranasal vaccine.

practice.stem: Order: doxycycline PO for a 6-year-old child after a tick bite. What should the nurse do?
options: Question the order — doxycycline is not given under age 7
Give it as ordered; the age limit applies only to ciprofloxacin
Give it at bedtime with a small sip of water
Give it with milk so it's gentler on a child's stomach
practice.rationale: Her rule: doxycycline "should never be given to children under the age of 7 because their baby teeth are still developing." Milk binds it, and a sip at bedtime risks esophageal injury.

practice.stem: Order: ciprofloxacin PO. Medication list: tizanidine. The nurse should:
options: Give both; only minerals and antacids interact with cipro
Give them at least 2 hours apart, like the mineral supplements
Hold the dose and contact the provider — they're contraindicated together
Give the cipro with a calcium supplement to protect the stomach from irritation
practice.rationale: "There is one drug, tizanidine, that is contraindicated with ciprofloxacin. Those should never be given together." Spacing doses fixes the mineral interaction, not this one.

practice.stem: Order: metronidazole PO. Medications: warfarin; INR today 2.6. Which action is most appropriate?
options: No change in monitoring — metronidazole doesn't affect warfarin
Monitor INR and bleeding closely; teach no alcohol for 3 days after
Give vitamin K with each metronidazole dose to prevent bleeding
Hold the warfarin until the course is done, on the nurse's authority
practice.rationale: Metronidazole increases warfarin's anticoagulant effect, so INR and bleeding are watched more closely; the alcohol teaching applies to every metronidazole patient. Warfarin changes are the provider's decision.

practice.stem: Amphotericin B, day 9. Creatinine 0.8 → 1.6 mg/dL; K⁺ 3.0 mEq/L (low); Mg²⁺ low; urine output falling. Next dose due in 1 hour. The nurse should:
options: Give the dose faster so the kidneys are exposed for less time
Give the dose — these values are expected and need no action
Hold all IV fluids to protect the potassium and magnesium
Report the lab trends and falling urine output before the dose
practice.rationale: Cumulative ampho B toxicity shows up as rising creatinine, low K⁺ and Mg²⁺, and declining urine output — the slide says report declining urine output or increasing creatinine. Never infuse faster than prescribed.

practice.stem: Order: azithromycin PO. A 66-year-old woman takes fluconazole; K⁺ 3.2 mEq/L (low). Which concern should the nurse raise?
options: Azithromycin will be inactivated by the fluconazole
Additive QT risk: two QT drugs, low K⁺, female
Risk of Achilles tendon rupture from the combination
Risk of serotonin syndrome from the combination
practice.rationale: Azithromycin and fluconazole both prolong the QT interval; hypokalemia adds risk; and women have a longer baseline QT. Tendons are cipro; serotonin syndrome is linezolid.

practice.stem: Order: linezolid IV. Medication reconciliation shows the patient takes sertraline (an SSRI) daily. The nurse should:
options: Give linezolid with a tyramine-rich meal
Give both and expect hyperkalemia
Notify the provider about the interaction risk (serotonin syndrome) before giving it
No action needed — linezolid interacts only with other antibiotics, not antidepressants
practice.rationale: Linezolid has MAO-inhibitor activity; with SSRIs/SNRIs and other psych meds it can cause serotonin syndrome — "complete a careful medication reconciliation." Tyramine-rich food is another interaction, not a fix.

practice.stem: Order: amoxicillin PO. Allergy list: "penicillin — hives and throat swelling." The nurse should:
options: Give half the dose first and observe for a reaction
Hold and contact the provider — allergy to one penicillin covers all
Give it with food, which prevents an allergic reaction
Give it; amoxicillin is a different class from penicillin, so no cross-allergy
practice.rationale: Hives and throat swelling describe a true reaction, and an allergy to one penicillin is an allergy to all of them (-cillin = penicillin). Food reduces GI upset with Augmentin, not allergy.

clinical.title: Scenario 1 — Emergency department
clinical.text: A 68-year-old man arrives from home, confused, with a 2-day history of fever and painful urination. Vitals: T 39.2°C, HR 118, BP 88/52, RR 24. The provider suspects sepsis and orders: blood cultures ×2, urine culture, piperacillin/tazobactam (Zosyn) IV now. No antibiotics have been given yet.

questions.stem: Put the nurse's actions in order.
options: Collect the blood and urine cultures with careful technique
Hang the first dose of piperacillin/tazobactam
Check which cultures are ordered and whether they have been drawn
Follow up on the culture and susceptibility results over the next 24–48 hours
questions.rationale: Cultures come before the first dose — "once the first dose goes into the patient, then our results are not accurate" — but without delaying a time-sensitive dose in sepsis. Then follow results, because they may change the drug.

questions.stem: Why is piperacillin/tazobactam a reasonable empiric choice here?
options: Organism unknown + severe infection → broad coverage, including Pseudomonas
It is an oral drug that can be given quickly in the ED
It is the narrowest penicillin available, so it spares his normal gut flora
It is the drug of choice for MRSA in septic patients
questions.rationale: Empiric therapy is the best guess for a severe infection with an unknown bug; sepsis gets broad antibiotics "as quick as possible." Zosyn is broad, IV, and covers Pseudomonas. It doesn't cover MRSA (that's vancomycin, linezolid, ceftaroline).

questions.stem: Twenty minutes later the lab reports a Gram stain from the urine. What does this result tell the team?
options: The exact organism and every antibiotic that it is susceptible to
Gram-positive vs gram-negative — not yet which drugs will work
Whether the patient has a true penicillin allergy
That the empiric antibiotic is already working
questions.rationale: A Gram stain comes back in about 15–20 minutes and only separates gram-positive from gram-negative. Identification and susceptibility take 24–48 hours.

questions.stem: At 48 hours he is improving. The culture grows one organism that is susceptible to several narrower drugs. What should the nurse anticipate?
options: Adding vancomycin for broader coverage
Reassessment and narrowing to targeted therapy
Continuing Zosyn for the whole course because it worked
Stopping antibiotics because he improved
questions.rationale: When results and the patient's response come back, the regimen is reassessed — continue, narrow, change or stop. Narrowing to a targeted drug spares normal flora and reduces selection pressure.

questions.stem: The lab reports the organism is "susceptible" to a drug. Which factors could still make that drug unsuitable for this patient? Select all that apply.
options: A serious past reaction to that drug
Kidney dysfunction that alters drug exposure
The drug has a long generic name
Infection in a walled-off abscess the drug penetrates poorly
A home medication that interacts with it
The drug is narrow spectrum
questions.rationale: "Susceptible" describes the organism and drug in the lab; the decision must also fit the site (CNS, bone, walled-off abscess) and the patient (reaction history, kidney/liver function, pregnancy, other medications). Narrow spectrum is a plus, not a problem.

clinical.title: Scenario 2 — Medical-surgical unit
clinical.text: A 45-year-old woman is admitted with pneumonia. Ceftriaxone (Rocephin) IV daily is ordered. Her chart lists "allergic to penicillin." She has one peripheral IV.

questions.stem: Which questions should the nurse ask to clarify the penicillin allergy? Select all that apply.
options: What exactly happened?
Which medication caused the reaction?
How soon after the dose did it happen?
Which pharmacy filled the prescription?
Was it the generic or the brand name?
Have you taken a penicillin or cephalosporin since without a problem?
questions.rationale: Slide 33's questions: which drug, what happened, how soon, how long ago, and whether she has tolerated a penicillin or cephalosporin since. "An itchy rash… is very different from my throat closed and I couldn't breathe." The pharmacy and brand don't change the risk.

questions.stem: She says, "As a teenager my throat got tight and I broke out in hives after amoxicillin." What is the nurse's best action?
options: Ask the provider to switch to amoxicillin/clavulanate (Augmentin) instead
Give the ceftriaxone — cephalosporins are a separate class
Document the reaction as a side effect rather than an allergy
Notify the provider first — cephalosporins carry some cross-sensitivity
questions.rationale: Throat tightness and hives describe a true reaction. A true allergy covers all penicillins (Augmentin included) and carries some cross-sensitivity with cephalosporins — the provider weighs the risk, and may still use it if the infection is severe.

questions.stem: The provider decides to continue ceftriaxone with close monitoring. When the nurse goes to hang it, her only IV has a calcium-containing solution running. What should the nurse do?
options: Y-site the ceftriaxone into the running calcium solution
Don't Y-site: stop, flush, give, flush — or use a separate line
Push the ceftriaxone quickly into that line so there's no time to react
Add the ceftriaxone directly to the solution bag
questions.rationale: Ceftriaxone with calcium-containing IV solutions forms a precipitate that can deposit in the lungs and kidneys. Her answer to "only one IV line?": give one, stop, flush, then give the other — never at the same time.

questions.stem: Ten minutes into the ceftriaxone infusion she develops wheezing and facial swelling. What should the nurse do first?
options: Stop the infusion
Give an antidiarrheal
Slow the infusion to half the rate
Finish the dose, then call the provider
questions.rationale: Signs of difficulty breathing, mouth/airway swelling, hypotension or hives → STOP THE INFUSION and notify the provider. This was the Kahoot item: "stop… and then notify the people who need to be aware."

clinical.title: Scenario 3 — Medical-surgical unit
clinical.text: A 19-year-old college wrestler who lives in a dorm has a large, draining abscess on his thigh with spreading cellulitis. T 38.6°C. Wound culture grows MRSA. IV vancomycin is started. Baseline creatinine 0.8 mg/dL.

questions.stem: Which features of his history fit community-associated MRSA?
options: Residence in long-term care
Contact sports and living in close quarters (a dorm)
Dialysis, an indwelling catheter and a recent hospital stay
Recent surgery
questions.rationale: CA-MRSA risks: contact-sport athletes, MSM, close quarters (prisons, military, college dorms). Dialysis, catheters, long-term care and recent surgery are healthcare-associated risks.

questions.stem: His mother asks why he can't just take amoxicillin. The best explanation is:
options: Amoxicillin can't reach the skin from the stomach
MRSA breaks down vancomycin, so penicillins fail too
MRSA's altered PBPs don't bind penicillins
Amoxicillin is only bacteriostatic — too weak for an abscess
questions.rationale: "The locks have been changed at all the doors" — MRSA's altered PBPs have low affinity for most β-lactams. Vancomycin works elsewhere in wall construction, so the altered PBPs don't matter.

questions.stem: Twenty minutes into the first vancomycin infusion his face and neck flush, he is itchy, and BP drops from 124/76 to 96/58. Put the nurse's actions in order.
options: Stop the infusion
Recognize flushing, itching and hypotension during the infusion as a reaction
Restart at a slower rate if the provider orders it
Notify the provider
questions.rationale: This is the histamine-release infusion reaction: it "can look like anaphylaxis, but it really isn't — you don't know that at the time," so stop, hold, contact the provider. Future doses may be restarted and infused more slowly.

questions.stem: Which monitoring belongs in his vancomycin plan? Select all that apply.
options: Tendon pain
Urine output
Serum creatinine trend
Weekly platelet count for serotonin syndrome
New hearing changes
A trough drawn right before the next dose
questions.rationale: "Really put together vanco and kidneys": creatinine, urine output, ordered levels (trough right before the next dose), plus ototoxicity. Serotonin syndrome and platelets are linezolid; tendon pain is ciprofloxacin.

questions.stem: On day 3 his creatinine is 1.4 mg/dL and his urine output has dropped. What should the nurse do?
options: Ignore it — one value doesn't matter
Switch him to oral vancomycin
Give the next dose faster to finish the course sooner
Report the trend to the provider before the next dose
questions.rationale: A rising creatinine from his own baseline and falling urine output signal nephrotoxicity — "a trend of anything is better than a one-time reading," and he has a trend. Oral vanco wouldn't treat a skin/soft-tissue MRSA infection.

clinical.title: Scenario 4 — Long-term care
clinical.text: An 82-year-old resident is on day 8 of clindamycin for a dental infection. Today she has had 7 watery stools with a strong, distinctive odor, abdominal cramping and T 38.3°C. Her daughter asks for an over-the-counter antidiarrheal.

questions.stem: What is the most likely explanation?
options: A delayed allergic reaction to the clindamycin
An expected, harmless side effect that will pass on its own
Resistance to clindamycin that she has developed
C. diff superinfection after clindamycin disrupted her flora
questions.rationale: "If nothing else, just be like, clinda → C. diff." Watery stools, cramping and fever fit; C. diff takes hold when normal flora are disrupted. Patients don't become resistant — bacteria do.

questions.stem: How should the nurse respond to the daughter's request?
options: Give the antidiarrheal only at night so she can sleep, then reassess
Tell her the diarrhea will stop once the course ends
Explain it shouldn't be given on our own — the provider needs to know
Give the antidiarrheal and recheck the stools tomorrow
questions.rationale: Slide 48: do not independently treat significant diarrhea with antidiarrheal medication; report watery or bloody stools, cramping or fever during and after therapy.

questions.stem: Which findings during or after clindamycin should be reported? Select all that apply.
options: Watery stools
Harmless dark urine
Metallic taste
Bloody stools
Abdominal cramping
Fever
questions.rationale: Report watery or bloody stools, abdominal cramping or fever. A metallic taste and dark urine are metronidazole effects.

questions.stem: C. diff is confirmed and oral vancomycin is ordered. A new nurse asks why it's oral. The best answer:
options: Oral vancomycin stays in the intestine, which is where this infection is
Oral vancomycin works by blocking ribosomes
Oral vancomycin is absorbed better than IV
Oral vancomycin is less nephrotoxic, so it can treat any infection safely
questions.rationale: "Route is really important": oral vanco isn't absorbed well, so it isn't for systemic infection — but "if you happen to have an intestinal infection, that's where you want the antibiotic to be."

clinical.title: Scenario 5 — Intensive care unit
clinical.setting: Post-op day 1 after surgery for a perforated bowel
clinical.text: A 56-year-old man had surgery for a perforated bowel with a mixed intra-abdominal infection. He is started on imipenem/cilastatin (Primaxin) IV. Home medications include valproic acid for a seizure disorder. Creatinine 1.0 → 1.7 mg/dL since admission.

questions.stem: Why is a carbapenem a reasonable choice for this infection?
options: Carbapenems are narrow, so they spare the gut flora
Broadest β-lactams — good for mixed infections and anaerobes
Carbapenems are the drug of choice for MRSA and VRE infections
Carbapenems are bacteriostatic and gentle on the gut
questions.rationale: Carbapenems are "our broadest" — used for mixed infections, can penetrate the gram-negative envelope, and are particularly effective against anaerobes. They are NOT effective against MRSA, and they're bactericidal.

questions.stem: What is the most important interaction for the nurse to report?
options: Imipenem can lower valproic acid levels → breakthrough seizure
The combination causes ototoxicity and hearing loss
Valproic acid inactivates the cilastatin in the kidney tubules
The combination raises potassium to dangerous levels
questions.rationale: Carbapenems can substantially reduce valproic acid concentrations — "one of the biggest risks for having a huge, horrible seizure." This was the Kahoot item about identifying valproic acid use first.

questions.stem: Which factors raise his seizure risk on imipenem? Select all that apply.
options: Taking the drug with food
Concurrent valproic acid
His rising creatinine
Male sex
Penicillin-binding protein changes
Excessive imipenem exposure
questions.rationale: Kidney impairment increases imipenem exposure; excessive exposure increases seizure risk; and lowered valproic acid levels remove his seizure protection. Food, PBPs and sex aren't listed risks.

questions.stem: Which nursing assessment is the priority each shift while he's on imipenem?
options: Skin checks for sunburn and photosensitivity reactions
Tendon pain, especially at the Achilles
Hearing and balance before each dose
Neurologic status — headache, confusion, seizures
questions.rationale: Imipenem causes neurologic disturbances (headache, confusion, seizures); the nursing implications are to review kidney function and the dose, assess neurologic status, and reassess broad coverage when microbiology returns.

clinical.title: Scenario 6 — Intensive care unit
clinical.text: A 63-year-old woman with a serious gram-negative infection is on gentamicin IV combined with a β-lactam. She is also receiving another nephrotoxic medication. Day 3: creatinine 0.9 → 1.5 mg/dL; urine output 25 mL/h. She says her ears have been ringing since last night.

questions.stem: Why might gentamicin be combined with another antibiotic?
options: The combination can give enhanced antibacterial action in a serious infection
Gentamicin is only bacteriostatic and needs a bactericidal partner to kill bacteria
To lower the risk of toxic reactions
To prevent C. diff
questions.rationale: Gentamicin may be combined when the combination provides enhanced activity; combination therapy is used for severe infections. Gentamicin itself is bactericidal, and combinations increase toxic and allergic risk.

questions.stem: Which findings suggest gentamicin ototoxicity? Select all that apply.
options: Tinnitus (ringing)
Hearing loss
Vertigo or dizziness
Metallic taste
Balance difficulties
Photosensitivity
questions.rationale: Ototoxicity: tinnitus, hearing loss, dizziness, vertigo, balance problems — and "may be irreversible," so report early. Metallic taste is metronidazole; photosensitivity is doxycycline, cipro and TMP-SMX.

questions.stem: What is the nurse's priority now?
options: Give the next dose early to stay in the therapeutic range
Stop all IV fluids
Report the rising creatinine, low urine output and new tinnitus to the provider
Reassure her that ringing ears are expected and temporary, and give the next dose
questions.rationale: Kidneys and ears "trend together." Her risk is up — another nephrotoxic drug, longer therapy — and she now has signs of both nephrotoxicity and possibly irreversible ototoxicity. Report new tinnitus and kidney changes.

questions.stem: Gentamicin levels are ordered. Which action is most important?
options: Give the dose, then draw the trough right afterward and document the time
Skip the level as long as the creatinine is normal
Draw the level whenever the lab arrives on the unit
Draw at the specified times, coordinated with the dose; document times
questions.rationale: Obtain ordered gentamicin concentrations at the specified times, coordinate administration and lab collection carefully, and document dose and level times accurately.

clinical.title: Scenario 7 — Primary care clinic
clinical.setting: Same-day visit after a tick bite
clinical.text: A 34-year-old woman found an attached tick 3 days ago and now has a spreading rash. Doxycycline PO is prescribed. She takes a daily calcium supplement and uses antacids for heartburn. She plans to spend the weekend outdoors.

questions.stem: Before she starts doxycycline, what should the nurse review? Select all that apply.
options: Swallowing ability or esophageal problems
Her age
Baseline hearing test
Antacids and supplements
Valproic acid use
Pregnancy status
questions.rationale: Before doxycycline: pregnancy status and age (teeth and bone), antacids/supplements (absorption), swallowing ability and esophageal risk. Valproic acid is the carbapenem interaction; hearing is gentamicin and vanco.

questions.stem: Which instruction best prevents doxycycline-related esophageal injury?
options: Chew the tablet well before swallowing it
Take it with an antacid to coat and protect the esophagus
Take it lying down with a small sip of water
Full glass of water, upright ≥ 30 min, not right before bed
questions.rationale: Full glass of water, upright ≥ 30 minutes, not immediately before bed. Antacids bind the drug and reduce absorption.

questions.stem: She asks whether she must stop her calcium and antacids. The nurse's answer:
options: Yes — stop them until the course is done
Yes — and switch to an iron supplement instead
No — take them a few hours apart from the doxycycline
No — take them at the same time to protect your stomach
questions.rationale: Aluminum, calcium, iron and magnesium bind doxycycline. Her answer in class: no need to stop them — separate them, "usually they say 2–3 hours." Iron binds it too.

questions.stem: Her 6-year-old son was bitten by a tick too. She asks if he can take some of her doxycycline. The nurse should say:
options: Yes, but only for 3 days instead of the full 10-day course
Yes, at half the dose because he's smaller
Yes, as long as he takes it with milk
No — not under age 7, and antibiotics are never shared
questions.rationale: Doxycycline causes permanent tooth discoloration and affects developing bone — "it should never be given to children under the age of 7." And: "Do not save leftover antibiotics or share them."

questions.stem: What should she do about her weekend outdoors?
options: Nothing special — doxycycline has no skin or sun-related effects
Use sun protection — doxycycline causes photosensitivity
Skip the doxycycline doses on the weekend days
Take a double dose before going outside
questions.rationale: Doxycycline causes photosensitivity: use sun protection (long sleeves, protective clothing) and report severe skin reactions. Don't skip or change doses independently.

clinical.title: Scenario 8 — Medical unit
clinical.text: A 70-year-old man has a wound infection with vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE). Linezolid (Zyvox) IV is ordered. His home medications include sertraline (an SSRI) for depression.

questions.stem: Why is linezolid being used?
options: It acts against VRE (and MRSA) and is protected for these resistant organisms
It is the broadest antibiotic for mixed infections, including anaerobes
It covers Pseudomonas
It is the preferred drug for C. diff
questions.rationale: Linezolid treats MRSA and VRE, so "let's protect this antibiotic and not use it for a whole bunch of other stuff." Broadest/mixed = carbapenems; C. diff = oral vanco; Pseudomonas = Zosyn, cefepime, cipro.

questions.stem: Medication reconciliation finds the sertraline. What should the nurse do?
options: Notify the provider of the risk of serotonin syndrome with linezolid
Give both — they don't interact
Hold the sertraline permanently on the nurse's own authority and document
Give the linezolid with a tyramine-rich meal
questions.rationale: Linezolid has MAO-inhibitor activity, so it interacts with psych medications like SSRIs and SNRIs — "complete a careful medication reconciliation." Stopping a home medication is the provider's decision; tyramine-rich food is another interaction.

questions.stem: Which findings could signal serotonin syndrome? Select all that apply.
options: Metallic taste
Tinnitus
Muscle rigidity
Diaphoresis
Tremor
Agitation
questions.rationale: Slide 49: monitor for agitation, confusion, diaphoresis, tremor, fever or muscle rigidity — "that's the serotonin syndrome." Tinnitus is ototoxicity; metallic taste is metronidazole.

questions.stem: On day 10 his platelet count has dropped. Which assessment finding is most concerning?
options: A sunburn
Dark urine with no other new symptoms or bleeding
Ringing in the ears
Bleeding gums and oozing at the IV site
questions.rationale: Linezolid causes myelosuppression, especially thrombocytopenia — so the CBC is monitored and the nurse looks for bruising and bleeding: gums, blood in the urine, oozing from the IV site.

clinical.title: Scenario 9 — Clinic, then emergency department
clinical.text: A 72-year-old woman with a complicated urinary tract infection is prescribed ciprofloxacin PO. She takes prednisone daily, a multivitamin with minerals, antacids, tizanidine for muscle spasms, and has reduced kidney function and type 2 diabetes.

questions.stem: Which of her characteristics raise her risk of fluoroquinolone tendon injury? Select all that apply.
options: Type 2 diabetes
Reduced kidney function
Age 72
Daily prednisone
Taking a multivitamin
questions.rationale: Tendon-injury risk increases with older age, concurrent corticosteroids, kidney/heart/lung transplant, and kidney impairment. The multivitamin matters for absorption, and diabetes for dysglycemia — not tendons.

questions.stem: Which medication on her list must the nurse raise with the provider before the first dose?
options: The multivitamin — it must be stopped permanently
Prednisone — it inactivates ciprofloxacin in the gut
Tizanidine — it is contraindicated with ciprofloxacin
None of them
questions.rationale: "Tizanidine… is contraindicated with ciprofloxacin. Those should never be given together." Prednisone raises tendon risk (teach about it), and minerals are separated by several hours, not stopped.

questions.stem: How should she take the ciprofloxacin with her multivitamin and antacids?
options: Take them all together with breakfast
Stop the multivitamin forever
Take the antacid first to protect the stomach, then cipro right after
Separate them by several hours
questions.rationale: Aluminum, calcium, iron, magnesium and zinc reduce oral cipro absorption — "separate those by several hours orally so that they don't combine in the stomach."

questions.stem: On day 4 she comes to the ED with sudden pain and swelling at the back of her ankle. What does the nurse suspect?
options: C. diff
A photosensitivity reaction from the ciprofloxacin
Achilles tendinitis or rupture from ciprofloxacin
An infusion reaction
questions.rationale: Fluoroquinolones cause tendinitis and tendon rupture — "usually the Achilles," which means "significant surgery and recovery." Tendon pain or swelling is reported promptly.

questions.stem: Her home glucose readings have been unusually erratic since starting cipro. The nurse recognizes:
options: Hyperkalemia from the antibiotic
An expected effect of her multivitamin
A sign that the infection is cured
Dysglycemia from cipro — report it
questions.rationale: Cipro's serious adverse effects include tendinitis/rupture, peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects, dysglycemia and QT prolongation; glucose is part of the pre-administration risk review.

clinical.title: Scenario 10 — Primary care
clinical.setting: Start of TMP-SMX and follow-up on day 3–5
clinical.text: A 66-year-old man is prescribed trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (Bactrim) for a susceptible infection. Medications: lisinopril (an ACE inhibitor, which raises potassium) and warfarin. No heart or liver failure.

questions.stem: Which values should be monitored during his TMP-SMX therapy? Select all that apply.
options: Potassium
INR
Kidney function
Valproic acid level
Vancomycin trough
CBC
questions.rationale: Monitor potassium (hyperkalemia), kidney function (injury, crystals), CBC (marrow suppression) and INR because TMP-SMX increases warfarin's effect. Troughs and valproic acid belong to other drugs.

questions.stem: Before the first dose, which allergy question is most important?
options: "Have you ever reacted to penicillin or a cephalosporin?"
"Do you have a latex allergy?"
"Have you ever reacted to a sulfa (sulfonamide) medication?"
"Are you allergic to calcium?"
questions.rationale: Sulfa-containing compounds are a somewhat common allergy, so ask specifically about sulfonamide reactions — not just this drug.

questions.stem: On day 3 his K⁺ is 5.6 mEq/L (high). The nurse recognizes:
options: Hyperkalemia from TMP-SMX plus lisinopril — report it
An expected value from lisinopril alone that needs no action
Hypokalemia caused by the TMP-SMX
A lab error caused by the warfarin
questions.rationale: TMP-SMX can cause hyperkalemia, and the risk climbs with other medications that increase potassium (ACE inhibitors among them). "Now our risk is increasing."

questions.stem: On day 5 he calls with a spreading rash and painful sores in his mouth. What is the nurse's priority?
options: Apply sunscreen and continue the drug
Prompt evaluation — rash with mouth sores may be SJS
It's thrush — swish nystatin and continue the TMP-SMX
Double his fluids and wait a week
questions.rationale: TMP-SMX can cause Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis — "a really bad skin reaction that can be fatal." Rash or mucosal lesions are assessed promptly.

clinical.title: Scenario 11 — Oncology unit
clinical.text: A 58-year-old woman receiving chemotherapy for leukemia is severely immunosuppressed and has an invasive fungal infection. Amphotericin B IV is started. She also has oral thrush (nystatin suspension ordered) and takes warfarin for a clot.

questions.stem: Thirty minutes into her first amphotericin B infusion she has shaking chills, T 38.9°C, nausea and BP 92/54. What is happening, and what should the nurse do?
options: Expected — speed up the infusion so the reaction ends sooner
Anaphylaxis — this drug can never be given again
An infusion-related reaction — follow the protocol and notify the provider
Septic shock from the IV line — pull the line
questions.rationale: Fever, shaking chills, nausea and hypotension during or shortly after infusion — especially early doses — are infusion reactions: "like the flu times 10. It is miserable. It is not deadly." Follow protocol, notify for a significant reaction, and never infuse faster than prescribed.

questions.stem: Which should the nurse monitor during amphotericin B therapy? Select all that apply.
options: Intake and output
Tendon pain
Magnesium
Valproic acid level
Serum creatinine and BUN
Potassium
questions.rationale: Ampho B is nephrotoxic and wastes K⁺ and Mg²⁺: monitor creatinine/BUN, K⁺, Mg²⁺, I&O, CBC and liver tests. Valproic acid is the carbapenem interaction; tendons are cipro.

questions.stem: Two weeks in: creatinine 0.8 → 1.9 mg/dL, K⁺ 3.0 mEq/L (low), urine output falling, new muscle cramps. What do these findings suggest?
options: Cumulative ampho B toxicity — report UO and creatinine
The fungal infection has been cured
Hyperkalemia from the antifungal
An expected response to the nystatin plus the chemotherapy
questions.rationale: Rising creatinine, hypokalemia and falling urine output are the lab trends of ampho B nephrotoxicity; weakness, cramping and dysrhythmias are monitored because of the K⁺/Mg²⁺ losses. Report them — the meme: "Nephron… what happened?… Amphotericin B."

questions.stem: How should she take the nystatin suspension for her thrush?
options: Hold it until the IV antifungal is finished, then swallow it
Take it with an antacid
Swallow it right away so it is absorbed
Swish it around her mouth and hold it before swallowing
questions.rationale: Nystatin is inactivated once it hits stomach acid — "really a topical medication" — so it must stay in contact with the mouth. It treats local, not systemic, infection.

questions.stem: Later she is switched to fluconazole. Because she takes warfarin, the nurse should:
options: Expect the warfarin to stop working
Give fluconazole and warfarin at the same time to cancel each other out
Monitor INR more closely and watch for bleeding, plus liver function
No change — fluconazole has no interactions
questions.rationale: Fluconazole inhibits liver drug-metabolizing enzymes, increasing warfarin's effect and bleeding risk ("here we go with warfarin again"). It is also hepatotoxic, so liver tests are monitored.

clinical.title: Scenario 12 — Rapid rounds
clinical.setting: Quick patient questions across the clinic
clinical.text: Six patients, one question each. Read each stem on its own.

questions.stem: A patient finishing metronidazole today plans to have a beer at a party tomorrow night. The nurse says:
options: Alcohol is only a problem with the first dose
Wait at least 3 days after the last dose
One beer is fine if you eat food with it
Take an extra dose before the party
questions.rationale: Avoid alcohol during treatment and for at least three days after the final dose — it causes an Antabuse-like reaction: "if you drink it, you get sick."

questions.stem: A patient started on oseltamivir asks, "Since I'm taking Tamiflu, do I still need a flu shot?" The nurse says:
options: Yes — Tamiflu treats flu but isn't a vaccine; get both
No — Tamiflu protects you for the rest of the flu season
No — Tamiflu works as this year's vaccine
Only if you also catch a cold this winter
questions.rationale: "This is not a vaccine. This is just going to treat it if you do pick it up… you can get both." (Timing matters with the live intranasal vaccine.)

questions.stem: A patient on amoxicillin/clavulanate (Augmentin) complains of stomach upset. The best advice:
options: Take it with food
Stop it until the stomach settles
Take it with an antacid
Take it on an empty stomach
questions.rationale: Augmentin tends to cause GI upset, so take it with food — "their bellies will feel less sad." Stopping is a prescriber decision.

questions.stem: Before knee surgery, a patient asks why he's getting cefazolin when he has no infection. The nurse explains:
options: It treats an infection the surgeon suspects
It covers MRSA
It's a several-week course to prevent all infections after any surgery
It's surgical prophylaxis — a short, specific course to prevent infection
questions.rationale: Cefazolin is "frequently used for surgical prophylaxis." Prophylaxis must have a specific indication, drug, timing and duration — usually a few doses or days, "not several weeks." Ceftaroline is the MRSA cephalosporin.

questions.stem: A patient says, "I've taken so many antibiotics that I'm resistant to them now." The best response:
options: "Resistance only happens with broad-spectrum drugs."
"You'll need double doses from now on."
"Yes, your immune system now blocks antibiotics."
"The bacteria become resistant, not you."
questions.rationale: "Bacteria become resistant; the patient does not become 'resistant to antibiotics.'" Every antimicrobial can promote resistance — broad-spectrum ones are just more likely to.

questions.stem: A patient says she saved leftover amoxicillin from last year for her next sore throat and will share some with her sister. The nurse teaches:
options: Saving is fine as long as the pills aren't expired and stay sealed
Take the leftovers at the first sign of a cold
Sharing is fine within the same family
Don't save or share antibiotics — take them exactly as prescribed
questions.rationale: "Do not share or save antibiotics ever. That's universal." Antibiotics aren't for viral infections, and misuse adds to resistance — stewardship.

cards.front: Four things a drug must do to work
cards.back: Act on the organism · reach the infection site · stay active despite resistance · suit this patient
Drug hits the microorganism harder than the person — exploits bacterial vs human differences
Allergic reaction · damage to human tissue · disrupted normal flora

cards.front: Four bacterial target groups we study
cards.back: Cell wall · protein synthesis (ribosomes) · folate synthesis · DNA replication
Covers a smaller group — the best choice when the bug is known and susceptible; spares flora
Organism unknown, or several must be covered (e.g. ruptured appendix → gut bacteria in the peritoneum)
No — it covers more kinds of bacteria, and kills more normal flora
Drug inactivation · target alteration · reduced entry · efflux
Drug kills susceptible bacteria → a resistant mutant survives, faces no competition and multiplies

cards.front: Who becomes resistant — patient or bacteria?
cards.back: The bacteria. "It's not the patient."
All can — broad spectrum most likely; more use → faster resistance
BEFORE the first antibiotic dose (as long as it doesn't delay treatment)

cards.front: Why cultures before the first dose?
cards.back: "Once the first dose… goes into the patient, then our results are not accurate"

cards.front: Gram stain — what and how fast?
cards.back: Gram-positive vs gram-negative · back in ~15–20 min

cards.front: How long does a culture take?
cards.back: 24–48 hours — start broad, then tailor
Shows which drugs are likely to inhibit the isolated organism (petri dish: bigger clear circle = more effective)
Best-guess treatment before the organism is known (source, severity, local resistance, patient factors)
Changing the drug based on culture & sensitivity — continue, narrow, change or stop
New infection during treatment — normal flora killed, a second bug (C. diff, yeast) flourishes
Which drug · what happened · how soon · how long ago · tolerated a PCN/ceph since?
Take exactly as prescribed · call before stopping · don't save or share leftovers

cards.front: "Always finish all your antibiotics" — her update
cards.back: "Really just follow the directions" — C&S may change the plan
Penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems (not vancomycin)
Bind PBPs → no peptidoglycan cross-linking → wall weakens → bacterium dies (bactericidal)
Bacterial enzyme that cleaves the β-lactam ring → drug can't bind PBP
Altered PBPs — "the locks have been changed at all the doors"
~30% carry S. aureus · only ~1–2% carry MRSA
-cillin
Augmentin · take with food (GI upset)
Zosyn · broad, common IV, covers Pseudomonas
Block β-lactamases so the paired penicillin reaches its PBP · useless alone
10% report · ~1% truly allergic

cards.front: True allergy to one penicillin means…
cards.back: Allergic to all penicillins + some cross-sensitivity with cephalosporins
STOP the infusion, then notify the provider
Some penicillins ↓ methotrexate elimination → toxicity
cef- / ceph- · ceftriaxone (Rocephin)
Surgical prophylaxis
Cefepime → Pseudomonas · ceftaroline → MRSA (binds the altered PBP)
Precipitate → deposits in lungs & kidneys; fatal in infants — never together in one line
Allergy (PCN cross!) · thrombophlebitis · rare hemolytic anemia · diarrhea/C. diff
Imipenem/cilastatin (Primaxin) · broadest β-lactam, mixed infections, anaerobes — NOT MRSA
Blocks the KIDNEY enzyme that breaks down imipenem
Valproic acid levels drop → breakthrough seizures

cards.front: Vancomycin class & why it beats MRSA
cards.back: Glycopeptide, not a β-lactam — binds peptidoglycan building blocks, not PBPs
IV → systemic (MRSA) · oral → not absorbed → intestinal C. diff only
"Really put together vanco and kidneys" — creatinine, BUN, urine output

cards.front: When is a vanco trough drawn?
cards.back: Right before the next dose (lowest point)
Histamine: flushing, itching, hypotension → stop, notify; restart slower
Bacterial 70S vs human 80S — she: "just know that it's the ribosomes"
30S: doxycycline, gentamicin · 50S: azithromycin, clindamycin, linezolid
A functioning immune system to finish the job → avoid in immunocompromised
Gentamicin — misread mRNA → abnormal proteins
Vibramycin · full glass of water, upright 30 min, not at bedtime, sun protection

cards.front: Doxycycline — who should never get it? (her rule)
cards.back: Pregnant women and children under 7 (permanent tooth discoloration, bone)
Al, Ca, Fe, Mg bind it — separate ~2–3 h; no need to stop them
Zithromax · QT prolongation → fatal dysrhythmia (also hepatotoxicity)
Other QT drugs · low K⁺ or Mg²⁺ · rhythm disorders · women (longer baseline QT)
Clinda → C. diff (Cleocin)
Zyvox · MRSA and VRE (a protected drug)
Serotonin syndrome: agitation, confusion, diaphoresis, tremor, fever, rigidity
Thrombocytopenia → CBC; watch gums, urine, IV-site bleeding
Nephrotoxicity + ototoxicity (tinnitus, vertigo, hearing loss — may be irreversible)
Bacterial DNA replication (DNA gyrase/topoisomerase IV) · bactericidal
Tendinitis / tendon rupture, usually the Achilles
Older age · corticosteroids · kidney/heart/lung transplant · kidney impairment
Avoided under age 18 (tendon rupture risk)
Tizanidine (contraindicated)

cards.front: Metronidazole — trade name & harmless effects to warn about
cards.back: Flagyl · metallic taste, darkened urine
Antabuse-like reaction — avoid during and ≥ 3 days after
Bactrim, Septra · blocks two sequential steps of bacterial folate synthesis
SJS/TEN · marrow suppression · hyperkalemia · kidney injury/crystals · liver

cards.front: TMP-SMX — ask before the first dose
cards.back: Sulfa (sulfonamide) allergy
Metronidazole · TMP-SMX · fluconazole → ↑ INR/bleeding

cards.front: Why fungi are hard to treat
cards.back: Eukaryotic like us → fewer targets, more toxicity, long treatment
Diflucan · inhibits ergosterol synthesis · fungistatic
Hepatotoxicity, QT · ↑ warfarin effect
Binds ergosterol → membrane pores → fungicidal
Fever, shaking chills, N/V, headache, hypotension — "flu times 10… not deadly"
Creatinine/BUN · K⁺ & Mg²⁺ (both drop) · CBC · LFTs · I&O
Locally only — swish and hold (inactivated by stomach acid); thrush, skin
Tamiflu · neuraminidase inhibitor — new flu viruses aren't released
Start ASAP, within 48 h of symptoms (severe/hospitalized/high-risk may still benefit later)
Not a vaccine — get both; may interfere with the live intranasal vaccine

qa.q: (student asked) [question not audible — about resistance]
qa.a: "I'm going to get to that. I have a whole slide on that" → selection pressure and resistance development (slides 11–12).

qa.q: (student asked) Does the β-lactam work on MRSA?
qa.a: No — "the β-lactam ring cannot bind to the PBP, so it's basically ineffective."

qa.q: (student asked) How common is MRSA — are healthcare workers carriers?
qa.a: About 30% of people carry S. aureus, but only about 1–2% carry MRSA. "I would guess that a lot of healthcare workers are colonized."

qa.q: (student asked) Can colonizing staph turn into an infection?
qa.a: Yes — any staph you're colonized with can infect broken skin "in the right situation"; a MRSA strain is just harder to treat.

qa.q: Why is MRSA such a big deal? Why do we have such a hard time attacking it?
qa.a: Our biggest gun for a long time worked on PBPs, and MRSA has totally different PBPs.

qa.q: (student asked) What if the allergy was reported years ago in childhood — "my mom told me I was allergic"?
qa.a: Clarify it — "we don't know that." Most of the time we just choose something other than a penicillin.

qa.q: (student asked) What if penicillin is the only option (e.g. syphilis)?
qa.a: Patients with anaphylactic reactions may be admitted to the ICU and given penicillin (desensitization), prepared for anaphylaxis.

qa.q: (student asked) Is C. diff contagious to healthy people?
qa.a: She didn't think it tends to be — "it can't take hold" unless the normal flora is disrupted. A student had caught it after a lot of antibiotics for a bad sinus infection.

qa.q: (student asked) How do you treat C. diff?
qa.a: More antibiotics — because it's still a bacterium — which disrupt the flora more. Fecal transplant (healthy stool into the patient) is being researched.

qa.q: (student asked) Can penicillin cause neurotoxicity?
qa.a: At really high concentrations it can cause neurotoxicity or seizures, "but it's pretty uncommon in any doses that we get."

qa.q: (Kahoot) How do β-lactam antibiotics weaken the bacterial cell wall?
qa.a: Answer not audible. They bind PBPs → no peptidoglycan cross-linking → wall weakens → osmotic lysis (from slide 25).

qa.q: (Kahoot) How does clavulanate work with amoxicillin?
qa.a: It's a β-lactamase inhibitor — "going to fight back against the resistance mechanism that some bacteria have developed."

qa.q: (Kahoot) What causes MRSA's resistance to most β-lactam antibiotics? (stem partly heard)
qa.a: Answer not audible. Altered PBPs with low affinity for β-lactams (from slide 29).

qa.q: (Kahoot) A patient develops wheezing and facial swelling during a penicillin infusion. What should the nurse do first?
qa.a: Stop the infusion, then notify — "pretty much any time we have some kind of a reaction."

qa.q: (student asked) Do cephalosporins bind the same PBPs?
qa.a: Yes — same PBPs, same general target; the rest of the molecule is different enough to be a separate class (different spectrum, affinity, ability to reach the PBPs).

qa.q: (student asked) Will the exam use generic or trade names?
qa.a: "If there is a test question, you will always get the generic. And if I provided you with the trade, I'll also usually throw the trade in there."

qa.q: (student asked) If someone has a severe penicillin allergy, would they get a cephalosporin instead?
qa.a: First look for something with no risk — there's crossover risk because the structures are similar. If the infection is really severe, it may be considered.

qa.q: (student asked) What if there's only one IV line for ceftriaxone and a calcium-containing solution?
qa.a: Use separate lumens if available; otherwise give one, stop, flush, then give the other sequentially.

qa.q: (student asked) Shouldn't this interaction be caught before it reaches the nurse?
qa.a: Yes — EMR alerts and pharmacy checks should catch it, but think of the Swiss cheese model: the nurse is the last layer, so know the really big ones.

qa.q: (student asked) Why is it dangerous in the line but not in the body?
qa.a: Concentration — in the line it's highly concentrated; once in the bloodstream it's diluted. Infants have "a lot less body to distribute through."

qa.q: (student asked) Why do creatinine and BUN reflect kidney damage?
qa.a: The kidneys normally clear them, so when they build up the kidneys aren't clearing as well.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Why is identifying valproic acid use important before giving imipenem-cilastatin?
qa.a: Carbapenems reduce valproic acid levels, so a patient with a seizure disorder can have seizures.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which form of vancomycin is used for intestinal C. difficile infection?
qa.a: Answer not audible. Oral vancomycin — it stays in the intestine (from slide 40).

qa.q: (Kahoot) A patient develops flushing and hypotension during IV vancomycin. What action is appropriate?
qa.a: Answer not audible. Stop the infusion and notify the provider; future doses may be infused more slowly (from slide 41).

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which finding is most concerning during IV vancomycin therapy?
qa.a: A kidney finding (rising creatinine, falling urine output) — "really put those together, vanco and kidney function."

qa.q: (student asked) With doxycycline, do antacids and minerals have to be stopped?
qa.a: No — just separate them in the GI tract, "usually they say 2–3 hours."

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which instruction is correct for oral doxycycline?
qa.a: Answer not audible. Take with a full glass of water and stay upright at least 30 minutes; not right before bed (from slide 46).

qa.q: (Kahoot) What is the greatest risk from azithromycin?
qa.a: Answer not audible. QT prolongation → dysrhythmia (from slide 47).

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which finding during or after clindamycin therapy requires follow-up?
qa.a: Diarrhea (watery or bloody stools) — "that really strong correlation between clinda and C. diff."

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which monitoring is most important during gentamicin therapy?
qa.a: Answer not audible. Kidney function (creatinine, urine output) and hearing/balance, with levels drawn at the specified times (from slides 50–51).

qa.q: (Kahoot) [stem not audible]
qa.a: Her only words: "That's a bacteriostatic antibiotic." Likely the item on needing a functioning immune system (from slide 45).

qa.q: (Kahoot) What does ciprofloxacin target in bacteria?
qa.a: DNA replication — "one of the two that we looked at that are going to be messing with DNA replication" (DNA gyrase/topoisomerase IV).

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which report requires immediate follow-up during ciprofloxacin therapy?
qa.a: Answer not audible. Tendon pain or swelling (from slide 56).

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which teaching is correct for metronidazole?
qa.a: Answer not clearly audible. Avoid alcohol (and propylene glycol) during treatment and for at least 3 days after the last dose (from slide 57).

qa.q: (Kahoot) [stem not audible — likely why TMP and SMX are combined]
qa.a: "The two different steps that they're working at, ultimately, getting more suppression" — they block two sequential steps of folate synthesis (from slide 58).

qa.q: (Kahoot) How does fluconazole inhibit fungal growth?
qa.a: It inhibits ergosterol synthesis — "remember, this is for a fungus," so not PBPs (from slide 64).

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which finding is most concerning during amphotericin B therapy?
qa.a: Answer not audible. Declining urine output or rising creatinine (nephrotoxicity), with low K⁺ and Mg²⁺ (from slide 66).

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which instruction is correct for nystatin oral suspension?
qa.a: Swish and hold it in the mouth before swallowing — "it's essentially topical" for oral and sometimes esophageal thrush.

qa.q: (Kahoot) How does oseltamivir limit the spread of influenza?
qa.a: It inhibits neuraminidase so new viruses aren't released. Her hint: most antivirals end in -vir.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which statement about oseltamivir is accurate?
qa.a: Start it as early as possible — "within 48 hours is really the cutoff for it being good."
